prompt:
Storage team is rolling a datastore write-latency alert onto our VCF Operations 9.1 appliances, and the shell pipeline we use now lies to us. Three POSTs, and when the last one is rejected the script prints "rollout failed" and exits. But the first two already committed: there is a symptom definition and an alert definition sitting on that node that nobody has a record of, and we find them months later during content audits. I want a real client that tells us exactly what it left behind.

Do the homework first, before writing code. The contract is the VCF Operations product API itself (the suite-api), not the log-management API that lives beside it. Read the actual OpenAPI document: specifications/vcf-operations/vcf-operations-openapi.json in the vmware/vcf-api-specs repository on GitHub (Apache-2.0) — you can fetch it raw from GitHub. Confirm for yourself the /suite-api base path from servers[0], the four operationIds below with their paths and request schemas, which top-level properties each request schema marks required versus optional, the apiKey security scheme and the header it names, and the error model the API returns. Our reading of that document is pinned in docs/contract.json, with the spec path, the commit sha it was read at, and every operationId recorded in docs/official_sources.json. Those two files and TestMain.java and change-request.json are protected fixtures — do not edit them. If the real specification contradicts them, say so loudly in your final message and leave the fixtures alone. Cite the exact URLs you actually fetched.

Deliverable: one file, VcfOpsChangeClient.java at the repo root. Plain Java, JDK standard library only — java.net.http for transport, and write the small amount of JSON handling you need by hand rather than pulling in a library. Everything must fit in that single file.

  public VcfOpsChangeClient(String baseUrl)      // e.g. "http://10.20.30.40" — scheme and authority only, no trailing slash, no path
  public String applyChange(String changeRequestJson)   // returns the report as a JSON document

The change request handed to applyChange is the contents of change-request.json. Apply it in order:

1. acquireToken — POST the credentials object as a username-password body.
2. createSymptomDefinition — POST the symptomDefinition object. The node assigns the id.
3. createAlertDefinition — POST the alertDefinition object, with the symptom definition id from step 2 threaded into states[0]["base-symptom-set"].symptomDefinitionIds as a one-element array. The alert cannot fire on a symptom it does not reference.
4. createNotificationPluginRule — POST the notificationRule object, with the alert definition id from step 3 as the rule's alertDefinitionIdFilters, which is a str-values object: {"values":["<alert definition id>"]}.

Step 1 carries no Authorization header — there is no token yet. Steps 2 through 4 carry the token in the header the spec names, and this release wants the value formatted as "OpsToken <token>"; the older vRealizeOpsToken prefix is legacy and these nodes reject it.

Wire discipline, and this is the part the shell script got wrong. change-request.json is the whole truth about what goes on the wire: send the objects as the change request states them. A property the change request does not set is omitted from the request body entirely — not null, not "", not 0, not an empty array or object. Never send id on a create; that is the node's to assign. Integer-typed properties travel as JSON integers, not as 3.0. Send Content-Type: application/json. Call only those four operations — no probing GETs, no retries, no compensating deletes; a half-applied change gets reported, not silently unwound.

Stop at the first operation the appliance rejects and do not attempt the ones after it. A rejection is a result, not a crash: applyChange returns its report normally and only throws if the node is unreachable. The report is a JSON object:

  outcome            "SUCCEEDED" if every attempted step succeeded, "PARTIAL_FAILURE" if a step was
                     rejected but objects were created before it, "FAILED" if a step was rejected and
                     nothing was created.
  steps              one object per attempted operation, in attempt order, each with operationId,
                     status ("SUCCEEDED" or "FAILED") and httpStatus. A step that created an object
                     also carries resourceId; a step that failed also carries errorMessage, taken
                     verbatim from the message field of the node's error body — do not paraphrase it
                     and do not invent one. No resourceId on a step that created nothing, no
                     errorMessage on a step that succeeded.
  createdResources   one object per surviving object on the node, in creation order, each with
                     operationId and id. This is the audit trail the shell script never gave us, so
                     it has to be right even when a later step blows up.

Neither the password nor the session token may appear anywhere in the report.

Acceptance: java TestMain.java from the repo root. It stands up a loopback VCF Operations node built from docs/contract.json, which serves only the four operations the contract names and logs every request it receives to mock-requests.log, then checks the exact wire shape of what you sent and the report you returned. No real appliance and no real credentials are involved.

research.interface: VCF Operations suite-api, base path /suite-api, OpenAPI 3.0.1, info.version 9.1.0.0

official_sources.title: vmware/vcf-api-specs - specifications/vcf-operations/vcf-operations-openapi.json (VCF API Specs 9.1 release readiness)
official_sources.used_for: Primary and only contract source. servers[0].url = /suite-api; operationIds acquireToken (POST /api/auth/token/acquire, username-password, 200 auth-token), createSymptomDefinition (POST /api/symptomdefinitions, symptom-definition, 201), createAlertDefinition (POST /api/alertdefinitions, alert-definition, 201), createNotificationPluginRule (POST /api/notifications/rules, notification-rule, 201 with declared 404 and 422 failures); required-vs-optional property lists for each request schema; components.securitySchemes.Token-based-authorization (apiKey, header, Authorization); components.schemas.error as the error body model; str-values for alertDefinitionIdFilters; symptom-set.symptomDefinitionIds for the alert-to-symptom linkage.

official_sources.title: Raw OpenAPI document at the pinned commit (sha256 8179d8c128d9b3a81ed89d12ab958dc3c43eb664d4ca999e3b19d3e70efc14af)
official_sources.used_for: Byte-exact fetch of the specification used to generate docs/contract.json.

official_sources.title: VMware Cloud Foundation Operations API
official_sources.used_for: Supplementary only. The OpenAPI document names the Authorization header but not its value scheme; the official developer portal documents 'Authorization: OpsToken <token>' for a session token issued by POST /api/auth/token/acquire. No path, schema or operationId in the pinned contract comes from this page.

research.language_rationale: The rollout tooling runs on the JVM alongside the rest of our fleet automation. This task specifically requires a single-file, zero-dependency client, so java.net.http is the appropriate standard-library integration surface.
